report.source_text: One day later, she consulted the general emergency department complaining of blurred vision in both eyes, headache, persistent genital lesions, lumbar pain, and recurrent fever (39 °C). Neurological examination was normal, with the exception of bilateral decreased visual acuity. The presence of retinal hemorrhages was suspected. C-reactive protein (CRP) was 204 mg/L and leukocytes 13.9 G/L. Repetitive hemocultures, white blood cell count, protein PCR and culture of cerebrospinal fluid from a lumbar puncture, PCR samples of vulvar lesions (HSV, chlamydia, and gonococcus), and serology results (Epstein-Barr virus (EBV, syphilis, Human Immunodeficiency Virus HIV)) were all negative. Given the suspicion of retinal lesions, the patient was advised to rapidly consult an ophthalmologist. As blurred vision can be a possible side effect of valaciclovir, the antiviral treatment was switched to acyclovir, and the patient was discharged.

report.source_text: fundoscopy showed bilateral parafoveolar microhemorrhages, and whitish lesions of the retina (Fig. 2A). Visual acuity was 0.3 (right eye) and 0.4 (left eye). Optical coherence tomography angiography revealed superficial and deep microangiopathy of the retina (Fig. 2B–D). Heidelberg spectral domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) of the paramacular lesion revealed a hyperreflectivity at the junction of the outer plexiform layer and inner nuclear layer, revealing a focal ischemia (Fig. 3). The diagnosis of Behçet’s disease was made, and intravenous corticosteroid treatment was initiated with pulsed 500 mg/day methylprednisolone infusion for 3 days, followed by systemic oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/day with a tapering schedule.

report.source_text: Progressive improvement of visual acuity and healing of vulvar ulcers were observed over the days following treatment initiation. Her estroprogestative pill was switched to a progestative-only pill owing to the risk of thrombosis associated with Behçet’s disease. The patient was discharged from hospital on day 4. Within 48 hours, a TNF blocking agent (intravenous infliximab 5 mg/kg/dose) was started. Visual acuity improved progressively. Infliximab was administered for a total of 4 months along with oral azathioprine up to 2 mg/kg/day. She will likely continue azathioprine for long-term maintenance, once corticosteroid tapering is completed. At the last visit, one and a half years after the initial symptoms, the patient had not experienced any relapse. At the last visit, Heidelberg SD-OCT (Fig. 3 right) showed atrophy of the macula. Besides, OCTA images remained unchanged, but the patient had recovered a vision of 1.0 (20/20) in both eyes.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 23-year-old previously healthy Western-European female presented to the gynecological emergency service with acute vulvar pain, edema, erosive papules, and fever (39.5°C). Initial clinical suspicion was HSV-2 infection, and a PCR swab was obtained. She was discharged with valaciclovir and NSAIDs. One day after initial presentation, she returned to the general emergency department with blurred vision in both eyes, bilateral decreased visual acuity, headache, lumbar pain, and persistent fever (39°C). Comprehensive infectious workup was negative (PCR for HSV, chlamydia, gonococcus; serology for EBV, syphilis, HIV; CSF analysis; blood cultures). By day 4, genital lesions had progressed to multiple painful deep ulcerations with dysuria and urinary retention, and blurred vision persisted. Ophthalmology evaluation on day 4 revealed bilateral parafoveolar microhemorrhages, whitish retinal lesions, visual acuity of 0.3 (right eye) and 0.4 (left eye), OCTA showing superficial and deep retinal microangiopathy, and SD-OCT demonstrating focal ischemia at the paramacular lesion—findings consistent with retinal vasculitis. Based on the constellation of recurrent genital ulcers and ocular involvement (retinal vasculitis), Behçet's disease was diagnosed on day 4. High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone 500 mg/day was administered for 3 days, followed by oral prednisone 1 mg/kg/day with tapering. Within 48 hours of discharge, intravenous infliximab 5 mg/kg/dose was initiated and continued for 4 months along with oral azathioprine up to 2 mg/kg/day. Progressive improvement of visual acuity and healing of vulvar ulcers were observed following treatment initiation. At 1.5 years follow-up, the patient had not experienced any relapse, had recovered visual acuity of 1.0 (20/20) in both eyes, and was maintained on azathioprine for long-term disease control.
